title: The summit
hookLine: the path goes on after the hill: every day's prayer is another step
tomorrow: the hill is climbed. what does day one look like the second time?

cards: A gym in January. A new notebook. The first clean page of a planner.
People love a fresh start. At an airport curb, a friend pulls over, pops the trunk, and before the suitcase is even out, holds up her phone: a text from her grandmother, for the flight.
It's the line her grandmother says over coffee every morning, from the Bible: his compassions fail not; they are new every morning. Read it twice.
Because the path you've climbed has its own word for mornings, and for what you do once you reach the top.

teach.b: Here's the question at the summit: when you've finished, what then? The Qur'an answers in two short verses, in Pickthall's words: "So when thou art relieved, still toil And strive to please thy Lord." Finished one thing?
Turn to the next. And elsewhere: serve your Lord until the certainty comes to you, which commentators read as death.

teach.h: NO FINISH LINE SHORT OF THE END.
teach.b: There's no finish line short of that. Remember the delayed gate and the jacket on the carpet, back at the start of this camp: the Prophet ﷺ said the deeds God loves most are the constant ones, even if small.

So the summit isn't a flag. It's a prayer that begins again: Allahu akbar, the Fatiha, bow, prostrate, rise, the same steps you learned at the bottom of the hill. Now the neighbor, in their own words.
That text at the curb comes from Lamentations, in the Bible that Jews and Christians share.
In the King James words: "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
The shared thing is real, and it's worth telling a friend tonight: both traditions refuse to let an ending be the end. Mercy renews; you begin again.

teach.h: GRIEF AND FAITHFULNESS; WORK AND STRIVING.
teach.b: And the honest difference: Lamentations is a poet's grief over a ruined Jerusalem, and the newness it sings belongs to God's faithfulness, found in the ashes.
The Qur'an's verse speaks to someone who has just finished well, and tells them: still toil.

how: Muslims pray every day for life, beginning each prayer with 'Allahu akbar'; on finishing a reading of the whole Qur'an, many begin again, and after Ramadan many keep a little of its practice going.

o: the place where the path ends for good
the top of the climb, where the path starts again
a mountain where the Prophet received revelation

games.q: who said it — tap the pairs.
p: his compassions are new every morning
the first words of each prayer

s: the Qur'an treats finishing a task as the end of striving
94:7-8: so when thou art relieved, still toil, and strive to please thy Lord.
in Lamentations, 'new every morning' is said in a time of grief
the book mourns a ruined Jerusalem, and finds faithfulness there.
Muslims, Jews and Christians mean exactly the same thing by beginning again
they share the hope that an ending isn't the end, and say it in their own words and stories.

games.q: you finish a goal you've worked on for a year, and the next morning you feel flat. what do 94:7-8 suggest?
o: rest for a long while; a finished goal has earned a long break.
turn gently to the next small thing; when you're done, still toil.
start the next goal at double the pace, to keep the feeling going.
games.why: 'so when thou art relieved, still toil.' and the deeds God loves most are the constant ones, even if small. begin again, small.

practice: If you pray, pray two units now, and let the first Allahu akbar be your day one, again. If you don't, stand for a moment, then sit, and let that be your first step.
Either way, before the time is up, name the first small thing you'll do tomorrow morning, and where in the morning it goes.

wordCard.voice: The summit: the top of the hill, where the path doesn't end. It turns, and starts again at the first step.

orig.note: Arabic: a unit of prayer: standing, bowing, prostrating, rising.

carryVoice: Your line: and begin again, from the very first Allahu akbar. Fifteen of fifteen, the summit, and the path goes on.
